_comment: Stable CheckId catalog. A CheckId stays the same across runs so that findings remain comparable. A CheckId carries no meaning: the prefix is the report section from config/sections.json, the number is a sequence number within that section and not a ranking. Ranking lives in 'defaultSeverity' and in config/rollout-waves.json. A number is never reused and never renumbered: a removed check leaves a permanent gap, and a reused number makes an old finding look like it belongs to a new check, which a run comparison cannot detect. 'category' is the meaningful axis: the Microsoft component where the administrator RESOLVES the finding, not where the problem originates. Allowed values are in config/categories.json; this value may change freely when Microsoft renames something, because the key is fixed and survives that naming. 'domain' refers to the design domain; it drives the raw/ folder structure and the log context, and it is the link back to the design, but deliberately does not appear in the report. 'reliability' determines whether a deviation is reported as Gap or Review required. 'learnUrl' (optional) is a verified learn.microsoft.com link to the Microsoft advisory article on which the check is based; only set it for a confirmed, current URL, never guess. 'selfDesigned' (optional, bool) marks a check that IS based on a concrete insight but is NOT traceable to one specific Microsoft Learn article (after actual research, not a guess). It is CAInventory's own insight or trade-off, not a placeholder to fill in later. It renders on the reference page as 'Own design' instead of a link. 'licenseRequirement' (optional, list) names the capabilities from config/sku-license-map.json of which AT LEAST ONE must be present for the check to be measurable; Test-CAInvLicensePrecondition otherwise sets the check to Not assessed without attempting the Graph call. Only fill this in for a license requirement that was actually verified with Microsoft, never on a suspicion: a wrong requirement silently makes a measurable check unmeasurable. 'title' (English, short check title), optional 'reviewQuestion' (for a Review required check: the question the administrator must answer) and 'description' (English explanation in plain language) live directly here. There is a single language, so no translation layer is needed. No em dashes in the texts.

checks.title: License coverage for CA controls
checks.reviewQuestion: Does this license cover the controls you want to enforce?
checks.description: Checks whether the tenant holds the licenses your planned controls need: Entra ID P1 for Conditional Access, P2 for risk and PIM, Intune for device compliance. No license means a control cannot be enforced compliantly, no matter how well you design it.

checks.title: Tenant basics and domains
checks.description: Records who the tenant is and which domains are verified. Baseline context. Pay particular attention to federated and onmicrosoft domains, since they help determine what your break-glass setup should look like.

checks.title: Federation behavior at MFA
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you trust the MFA claim this federated domain delivers?
checks.description: For a federated domain, federatedIdpMfaBehavior determines whether Entra trusts the MFA claim from the federation partner or enforces its own verification. If nothing is set, Entra falls back to accepting it: the MFA requirement in your Conditional Access policy is then, in practice, fulfilled by an external party, and that is rarely a deliberate choice. The check reads the setting per federated domain. If the tenant has no federated domains, the question does not apply.

checks.title: CA references a non-existent group
checks.description: A Conditional Access policy references a group that no longer exists or is soft-deleted. Such a dead reference makes the policy behave differently than intended: the target audience or the exclusion silently drops out.

checks.title: CA policy status recorded
checks.description: Records whether a policy is on, running in report-only mode, or off. Useful to know: report-only enforces nothing yet, it only observes.

checks.title: 'All users' without exclusions
checks.reviewQuestion: Is it deliberate that this policy excludes no one?
checks.description: An enabled policy hits everyone, with no exclusion at all. Usually fine, but if your emergency accounts also fall under it, a migration can lock everyone out in one stroke. If the break-glass set was supplied via -EmergencyAccountUpn, this is a proven Gap; without that set it remains a confirmation question. Report-only and step-up-only policies fall outside this check: they cannot block a sign-in.

checks.title: Terms of Use and authentication context
checks.description: Inventories Terms of Use and authentication contexts, and checks whether CA points to a deleted instance. If the object is missing, the policy does not do what you think it does.

checks.title: User and group population
checks.description: Counts members, guests, synced and cloud-only accounts, plus the number of groups. This determines the size and nature of your target audience for CA scoping.

checks.title: Possible service or shared account
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this a service or shared account, and should it fall outside the user scope?
checks.description: An account whose name resembles a service, shared, or test account. Those call for different CA treatment than a regular user, because they get stuck at a different moment. This is a name heuristic, so always confirm it yourself.

checks.title: CA exclusion group without an owner
checks.description: A group that excludes users in CA but has no owner. Without an owner, nobody is accountable for who ends up in the exclusion. This is considered the biggest hidden risk in CA standardization, and rightly so.

checks.title: Dynamic group with a processing error
checks.description: A dynamic group whose membership rule is not processed correctly. Membership can as a result be stale or incomplete, which skews your effective CA scope without you seeing it.

checks.title: CA group is not protected against self-addition
checks.reviewQuestion: May a regular group owner add themselves to this CA group?
checks.description: A group used in an enabled CA policy (include or exclude) is not role-assignable. For such a group, a regular group owner can add themselves or others to the CA scope or exclusion; for a role-assignable group that sits with Privileged Role Administrators by default, though management can genuinely be delegated by adding group owners. What is harder: changing credentials, resetting MFA, and editing sensitive attributes of members and owners requires at least the Privileged Authentication Administrator role. This is this module's own judgment call, not Microsoft advice: Microsoft nowhere ties role-assignable groups to Conditional Access scoping, actually recommends a regular dedicated security group for the break-glass exclusion, and explicitly states a CA group may be of any group type. So weigh yourself whether the risk here outweighs the constraints. Note: isAssignableToRole is immutable and can only be set at creation, so remediation always means a new group. Dynamic and on-prem synced groups can never become one by definition. Two constraints factor into that trade-off: nesting is not supported (a group cannot be a member of a role-assignable group), so CA scoping that relies on nested groups does not work here, and a tenant can have at most 500 role-assignable groups, which is a real ceiling for a large CA set with many exclusion groups.

checks.title: Number of permanent Global Admins
checks.reviewQuestion: Are all of these permanent Global Administrators actually needed?
checks.description: Counts the users with a standing Global Administrator role, i.e. not the temporary ones via PIM. Too many standing admins enlarges your attack surface. Microsoft recommends assigning the role to fewer than five people and itself shows a warning card on the Entra overview page from five assignments onward; this check follows that threshold and treats one to four permanent Global Admins as OK. How many of these admins are day-to-day admins and how many are emergency accounts is worked out by Identity-19, which runs later and does know the confirmed emergency account set. For the day-to-day admins: preferably eligible via PIM.

checks.title: Privileged user in an exclusion group
checks.reviewQuestion: Is it deliberate that this admin falls outside the policy?
checks.description: A user with an admin role is in a group excluded from CA. Sometimes deliberate, but it bypasses security policy for exactly the most sensitive accounts. Check whether that is really intended.

checks.title: Number of break-glass accounts
checks.reviewQuestion: Are these all the emergency accounts, or is one missing?
checks.description: Checks whether there are at least two emergency access accounts. Those prevent you from locking yourself out if a CA migration goes wrong. Microsoft recommends two, cloud-only, each with a phishing-resistant method that differs from what regular admins use: a passkey (FIDO2) is the recommended choice, certificate-based authentication the alternative if a PKI is already in place. An emergency account is therefore not exempt from verification; it must be able to sign in itself once mandatory MFA enforcement applies (Emergency-07 checks that registration itself). Note: break-glass cannot be reliably auto-detected, so only accounts you explicitly name (via -EmergencyAccountUpn or -EmergencyAccountId) or that match a break-glass name pattern get a hard verdict. A cloud-only admin is shown at most as a candidate, not labeled as break-glass.

checks.title: Break-glass is cloud-only
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this emergency account genuinely cloud-only and decoupled from on-prem?
checks.description: An emergency account should be cloud-only and not synced. That way an outage in your on-prem or hybrid chain does not drag your emergency access down with it.

checks.title: Break-glass excluded from CA
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this emergency account excluded from everything that can block a sign-in?
checks.description: Checks whether the emergency account is explicitly excluded from every CA policy that can block or restrict a sign-in. Report-only policies block nothing and do not need to exclude the emergency account; policies that only act on an authentication context or a user action likewise don't. If not, a policy can block your emergency account at exactly the moment you need it.

checks.title: Break-glass and registration campaign
checks.reviewQuestion: Can the emergency account be reached by the registration campaign?
checks.description: A CA exclusion does not automatically stop a registration campaign (proof-up). This check looks at whether the emergency account falls within the campaign's targeting, since that can still render emergency access unusable.

checks.title: Recent test sign-in for break-glass
checks.description: Checks whether the emergency account was tested recently, within the log window. An emergency account that is never tested often turns out not to work in a crisis: an expired credential, a missing method. Microsoft states a cadence: validate that it works at least every ninety days, and again after changes to IT staff or subscriptions. Testing is the only way to avoid finding that out at the worst possible moment.

checks.title: Break-glass procedure (manual)
checks.reviewQuestion: Has the emergency procedure been tested and documented?
checks.description: Credential storage, PAW use, physical access, and the emergency procedure cannot be read from the tenant. This check flags that a human needs to validate this: vault, four-eyes, test report. Factor into that validation that Microsoft recommends the Global Administrator role for emergency accounts be permanently active and not eligible via PIM, since an activation itself requires working verification, and that there should be a validation round at least every ninety days.

checks.title: Break-glass has a phishing-resistant method
checks.reviewQuestion: Does this emergency account have a method that works during an outage?
checks.description: Since MFA became mandatory for the admin portals, an emergency account is no longer an account you exempt from verification: it must be able to sign in itself with a strong method. Microsoft recommends a passkey (FIDO2) or certificate-based authentication. This check verifies per confirmed emergency account whether such a method is registered, and flags it when both accounts share the same method. A Temporary Access Pass does not count.

checks.title: Emergency access without dependency on PIM
checks.description: Checks whether there is still a way in that does not depend on a PIM activation. Microsoft prescribes that emergency accounts get the Global Administrator role permanently active and not eligible, and itself names the opposite situation as a lockout scenario: if every assignment is eligible and activation fails, nobody can reach tenant administration anymore. If there is not a single permanent Global Admin, or the permanent roles sit with day-to-day admins but not with a confirmed emergency account, that is a Gap. Emergency-02 cannot report this: it judges per confirmed emergency account and stays silent precisely when there is none, while that is exactly when the question is most urgent.

checks.title: Break-glass uses the .onmicrosoft.com domain
checks.reviewQuestion: Does this emergency account have a UPN on the .onmicrosoft.com domain?
checks.description: Microsoft recommends the .onmicrosoft.com domain for an emergency account's UPN, separate from being cloud-only (Emergency-02): that domain cannot be federated and does not depend on DNS, so it keeps working if an outage in your own domain or federation is exactly the reason you need break-glass. A cloud-only account can still have a UPN on your custom domain and then misses that independence.

checks.title: Cross-tenant trusts external MFA or device
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you trust the MFA and device claims from this partner tenant?
checks.description: Checks whether the tenant trusts MFA or device compliance from an external partner tenant (cross-tenant inbound trust). Precheck: without guests in the tenant this does not apply, and this check shows Ready instead of a forced Review required.

checks.title: External identities and guests
checks.description: Inventories cross-tenant settings, external identity providers, and the number of guests. Baseline context for guest CA and collaboration risk.

checks.title: App exclusion in a CA policy
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this app exclusion still deliberate and justified?
checks.description: Lists the applications excluded from a CA policy, by name and not just their appId. Every exclusion is a deliberate gap in the policy and should be confirmed as such. Factor in service dependencies: cloud apps rely on each other, so a policy on one app carries through to another. Anyone using Microsoft Teams also falls under the policy on SharePoint Online and Exchange Online, because Teams calls those resources. That is not visible from the policy configuration itself and is a known source of surprises with app-targeted policies. The ownership check per excluded app runs via Foundation-14.

checks.title: Diagnostic settings for Entra logs
checks.reviewQuestion: Are the logs being written to where you need them?
checks.description: Checks whether Entra sign-in and audit logs flow to a Log Analytics workspace via diagnostic settings. Without that pipeline you're stuck with Graph retention, and that is license-dependent: seven days on Entra ID Free, thirty days on P1 and P2. With a workspace you can look back over a much longer window.

checks.title: Effective log window (retention)
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this lookback window enough to be able to demonstrate the rollout?
checks.description: The window you can actually use for usage analysis. If there's a readable Log Analytics workspace, the desired window extends up to the workspace retention, with a ceiling (-MaxLookbackDays). If there isn't, Graph retention applies and that is license-dependent: seven days on Entra ID Free, thirty on P1 and P2. If the window is shorter than requested, we say so honestly, because not measured is not the same as not used. Note that security signals have their own table (risky sign-ins seven, thirty, or ninety days depending on license; risky users with no limit); this window concerns the audit and sign-in logs.

checks.title: Registration campaign status and configuration
checks.description: Records whether the registration campaign (proof-up nudge) is on, which method is targeted, and how the include/exclude targeting looks. Baseline context for who gets hit by a registration nudge unprompted. Note: state 'default' means Microsoft-managed and in practice targets all MFA-capable users.

checks.title: Service account within the registration campaign
checks.reviewQuestion: Can this account complete a registration prompt?
checks.description: Checks whether heuristically recognized old-school service/shared accounts fall within the campaign scope. A non-interactive account cannot complete a proof-up nudge and gets stuck once the allowed snoozes run out. Exclusion must use DIRECT targeting: as an individual user in excludeTargets or as a direct member of the exclusion group, since the campaign ignores nested group members. Name heuristic, so always confirm.

checks.title: Direct members of campaign-targeted groups
checks.reviewQuestion: Does the campaign reach everyone you want it to reach?
checks.description: The registration campaign resolves group targeting on DIRECT members; nested group members don't count. This check tests every targeted group (include and exclude). Nested members of an exclusion group still get nudged (the exclusion doesn't work, so Gap). Nested members of an include group don't get nudged (possible coverage gap, so review).

checks.title: Security defaults status
checks.description: Checks whether security defaults are on. Security defaults and Conditional Access are mutually exclusive: if the defaults are on, your CA policies are not active. That makes it the most binary blocker in the whole model, since there is no scenario where a CA go-live succeeds while the defaults are on. The defaults must therefore be off before you cut over; this counts as a hard precondition for the go-live gate.

checks.title: Legacy per-user MFA
checks.reviewQuestion: Can the legacy per-user MFA policy be turned off?
checks.description: Measures per user whether legacy per-user MFA is still on (Enabled/Enforced) via the beta property perUserMfaState. Per-user MFA clashes with CA-enforced MFA and produces double prompts, so this should be off before Conditional Access takes over MFA enforcement. The accounts still set to it are named in the finding. If the measurement fails, the check becomes Not assessed with the portal as the fallback route.

checks.title: Legacy authentication usage
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this legacy traffic known, and can it be turned off?
checks.description: Counts observed sign-ins with a legacy client (IMAP, POP, SMTP, MAPI, ActiveSync, Other clients) within the log window, based on an explicit list of clientApp names. An unknown or unrecognized clientApp doesn't count as legacy but is reported separately. Legacy protocols bypass MFA and CA. Without logs this is Not assessed and never Ready: an empty observation is not proof of non-use.

checks.title: Authentication methods policy per method
checks.reviewQuestion: Are the right authentication methods on for what you're about to require?
checks.description: Records per authentication method whether it is on or off and how the targeting looks. This is the 'allowed' axis of the method matrix: what the tenant policy permits, independent of what users have registered or use. Newer methods are often beta.

checks.title: Authentication methods policy migration status
checks.description: Checks whether the tenant has moved management of authentication methods from the legacy MFA and SSPR policy to the authentication methods policy. Only at Migration Complete is the authentication methods policy authoritative and are the legacy settings ignored; before that they still count. If the tenant is still at premigration or migrationInProgress, the method matrix measures a policy that in practice is not solely determinative.

checks.title: Temporary Access Pass as a bootstrap path
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to use Temporary Access Pass to bootstrap people?
checks.description: A Temporary Access Pass is a temporary code that lets someone without a registered method sign in anyway and register a strong method from there. Microsoft explicitly intends it for that. Without that path, a phishing-resistant policy for anyone who hasn't registered anything yet isn't a tightening but a closed door, and that hits both admins without a method and the tail of the user population. Note: a Temporary Access Pass itself is not phishing-resistant, so bootstrapping must be finished before you enable such a policy.

checks.title: Authentication strengths
checks.description: Inventories the authentication strength policies and their allowed combinations, and whether they're referenced from CA. This is the 'eligible' axis of the method matrix: a method is only strength-eligible if it appears in the allowedCombinations of a strength in use.

checks.title: Registration readiness
checks.description: Summarizes the userRegistrationDetails report: how many users are MFA-registered, passwordless-capable, and phishing-resistant. Use this as a readiness report, not as the sole source of truth: it includes reporting latency.

checks.title: Users needing review
checks.reviewQuestion: Which of these users do we help before the wave opens?
checks.description: Counts users who are MFA-capable but not registered, or an admin without a phishing-resistant method. An MFA-capable but unregistered user gets stuck once CA enforcement kicks in; an admin without a strong method is elevated risk.

checks.title: Method minimum level per user
checks.description: Checks per user the strongest registered method against a floor (config/method-strength-map.json). By default that floor is Microsoft's built-in Multifactor authentication strength: below the minimum then means none of the registered methods counts toward MFA, i.e. this user cannot do MFA at all once enforcement kicks in. Set defaultMinimumWeight to a number to enforce a stricter weight threshold instead (SMS/voice < TAP < OTP < push < phishing-resistant); that relative ordering is this module's own judgment call, not a Microsoft classification, since Microsoft itself treats those three as equivalent. A Gap record per user below the minimum, plus an aggregate. An unknown method type never drops a user below the minimum as long as Graph itself reports isMfaRegistered, and is logged separately.

checks.title: Individual authentication methods
checks.description: Counts the registered method types per user. Sensitive in nature: phone numbers are always masked and the details are only fetched with -IncludeSensitiveMethodDetails. Microsoft's own API overview advises against this per-user call for tenant-wide audit/reporting (it's meant for user-management scenarios); that's why userRegistrationDetails (6.8/URD) without the flag remains authoritative for readiness.

checks.title: Self-service password reset
checks.reviewQuestion: Is self-service password reset set up as intended?
checks.description: SSPR is only partly readable via Graph: the enablement status, target audience, and password writeback remain largely portal-dependent. This check flags that a human needs to confirm this. SSPR and MFA registration share methods; a combined registration avoids double nudges.

checks.title: Method matrix per method
checks.description: Combines four axes per method: allowed (policy), registered (report), eligible (strength), and used (sign-ins). Answers at a glance what you can turn off and who that affects. If sign-ins are missing, the usage axis is Not assessed and never zero.

checks.title: Phase-out candidate (method)
checks.reviewQuestion: Can this method be turned off, or is someone still using it?
checks.description: A method that is on and registered, but shows no observable usage within the window. Candidate for phase-out, low severity, always review: a long tail of occasional usage can fall outside the window.

checks.title: Used but not strength-eligible
checks.description: A method with demonstrable usage that does not appear in the allowedCombinations of the planned strength. That is a high-severity migration risk: those users lose their working sign-in method once it's enabled.

checks.title: Application and service principal population
checks.description: Counts the service principals and app registrations. Baseline context for the size of the app landscape that falls under, or is excluded from, Conditional Access.

checks.title: Workload identity population
checks.description: Distinguishes the non-human identities: managed identities and application service principals. Those fall outside user CA but within Conditional Access for workload identities, and are a blind spot in CA standardization.

checks.title: Risky service principals
checks.reviewQuestion: Are these workload identities known and expected?
checks.description: Checks whether there are workload identities with active risk (Identity Protection). Requires a Workload Identities Premium license (separate from Entra ID P2; not detectable from Graph, so no precheck up front, a missing license automatically results in Not assessed). Risky service principals should be caught by CA for workload identities.

checks.title: Day-to-day admins with a permanent Global Admin role
checks.description: Subtracts the confirmed emergency accounts from the number of permanent Global Administrators, so you can see how many people work day in, day out with a standing Global Admin role. Identity-09 counts the total and its text assumes two of those are emergency accounts; that check cannot verify that assumption, since it runs before the emergency accounts are determined. This check does the subtraction for real. It passes no judgment of its own: Microsoft draws its line at the total assignment count, not at this derived figure, so a threshold of its own would be a guess. Without confirmed emergency accounts the outcome stays Not assessed, because an unconfirmed set is different from an empty set. If there are zero permanent assignments, the outcome is simply zero: the subtraction is then moot and there is nothing to confirm.

checks.title: Guests against a device-requiring CA policy with no trust or exclusion
checks.reviewQuestion: Can your guests still sign in once this policy applies?
checks.description: Cross-checks an enabled, tenant-wide CA policy that requires a compliant device against the guest population and the cross-tenant trust settings (Identity-14). If the policy requires a compliant device, there are guests in scope, the policy does not explicitly exclude guests, and no partner tenant is trusted for MFA or device compliance, then no guest will be able to sign in under this policy: their device can never be made compliant for this tenant. If trust does exist with at least one partner, it's not certain that covers all guests.

checks.title: Authentication flows
checks.reviewQuestion: Should these authentication flows be allowed?
checks.description: Checks whether CA uses the authenticationFlows condition (device code flow, authentication transfer). Device code flow is a known phishing vector and should be explicitly restricted in a modern baseline.

checks.title: Device population
checks.description: Counts the Entra device objects and the Intune managed devices. Baseline context for device-based CA controls (require compliant/hybrid device).

checks.title: Compliance policy per platform
checks.description: Checks per platform (Windows, iOS, Android, macOS) whether there is an assigned device compliance policy. If it's missing for a platform, a CA control 'require compliant device' is meaningless for that platform.

checks.title: Compliance status of devices
checks.description: Counts how many Intune-managed devices are compliant. Based solely on /deviceManagement/managedDevices (literally Intune's own complianceState), so only actually managed devices count.

checks.title: Device registration and join
checks.reviewQuestion: Is it correct that devices may be registered this way?
checks.description: Reads who may register and join devices and whether MFA is required for that. First checks whether a CA policy with the 'Register or join devices' user action (urn:user:registerdevice) is active; if so, that policy is authoritative and the legacy tenant-wide toggle should be off (otherwise the CA policy is not enforced correctly, per Microsoft's own warning). Without such a policy, the legacy toggle remains the signal to assess: joining a device without MFA undermines 'require compliant/hybrid device' controls.

checks.title: Defender connector
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to use the Defender connection as a CA signal?
checks.description: Checks whether a mobile threat defense connector (e.g. Defender for Endpoint) is linked. Precheck: only relevant if the compliance policy actually uses device threat protection (reuses Device-02); without that dependency this check shows Ready instead of a forced Review required. If the endpoint or the license is missing, this is Not assessed.

checks.title: Named locations
checks.reviewQuestion: Do these named locations still match where people actually work?
checks.description: Inventories the named locations (IP ranges, countries), whether they are trusted, and whether they're referenced from CA. A named location that no CA policy points to is dead configuration: clean it up or actually put it to use. An unused trusted location is a risk if it later gets linked by accident.

checks.title: Session controls
checks.reviewQuestion: Do these session settings match how long a session should last?
checks.description: Summarizes the session controls from the CA policies: sign-in frequency, persistent browser, app enforced restrictions, cloud app security. Those determine how long a session stays valid: too tight causes prompt fatigue, too loose undermines the benefit.

checks.title: Global Secure Access and compliant network
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to use Global Secure Access as a compliant network?
checks.description: Checks whether the compliant network condition (Global Secure Access) is enabled and used by CA. Precheck via the automatically created named location "All Compliant Network Locations": if it's missing, the condition was never enabled and this check shows Ready instead of a forced Review required. If it does exist, this check never fails hard on the GSA endpoint itself; parts are preview or portal-only and vary by target cloud.

checks.title: Evidence readiness
checks.reviewQuestion: Will this let you demonstrate what happened later?
checks.description: Determines whether the log-dependent controls carry meaning: is the effective window equal to the desired one, and are there diagnostic settings. A window shorter than requested doesn't make log conclusions useless, but it does make them less far-reaching.

checks.title: Sign-in logs
checks.description: Summarizes the sign-ins within the window: total, failed, and with CA applied. The sign-ins feed the method matrix and the legacy auth check. Not measured within the window is not proof of non-use.

checks.title: CA coverage gap: traffic without Conditional Access
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this traffic without Conditional Access explainable?
checks.description: Exclusions are visible and deliberate; uncovered surface is invisible and usually unintentional. This check looks for the applications where interactive sign-ins occurred without a Conditional Access policy being applied, and looks at the result per policy. No policy evaluated at all is a genuine coverage gap; policies that were evaluated but whose conditions didn't hold can be a deliberate exclusion; policies that are all off is coverage that was designed but isn't switched on. Only measures interactive sign-ins within the log window.

checks.title: CA change history
checks.description: Counts the Conditional Access-related policy changes within the window. During a migration, the change history is the evidence that the baseline came about in a controlled way; undocumented changes are a governance risk.

checks.title: Risky users
checks.reviewQuestion: Have these risk signals been handled?
checks.description: Counts the users with active risk (Identity Protection, requires P2). Risk-based CA policies rely on these signals; without P2 they don't exist and every risk-based control is meaningless.

checks.title: Risk detections
checks.description: Counts the risk detections within the window (Identity Protection, P2). Context for how often risk-based CA would actually have fired in practice.

checks.title: Exclusion surface
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this exclusion documented with an owner, reason, and end date?
checks.description: Aggregates the exclusions the earlier layers already found: CA policies with exclusions and open exclusion-related findings. The technical scope is readable, the legitimacy usually isn't. Record owner, reason, end date, and approval per exclusion; without that metadata an exclusion is a finding.

checks.title: Governance and maintainability
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this governance point assigned and documented?
checks.description: The governance questions (design owner, change process, naming/documentation, test and rollback procedure) cannot be read from the tenant. This check flags that a human must confirm them from the manual register. Without documented governance, the baseline drifts unnoticed.

checks.title: Expiring Microsoft functionality
checks.reviewQuestion: Does this expiring functionality affect your setup?
checks.description: Checks the lifecycle dates from config/lifecycle-dates.json against the run date. Conditional Access relies on functionality Microsoft retires on fixed dates; an assessment that doesn't know those dates recommends a setup that breaks within a year. A date that has passed only becomes a gap once the linked checks show the topic is still relevant in this tenant, so a customer doesn't get warned about something that doesn't affect them. Upcoming dates within six months become a review point.

checks.title: Finding with an unknown CheckId
checks.description: Tests the check catalog itself, in two parts. First: does every finding from this run carry a CheckId that appears in the catalog? A record with an unknown id shows up in the report with no title, description, or source, and is unexplainable to the reader; that happens when a check is removed from the catalog while the collector that writes it stays in place. Second part: is the catalog's own taxonomy correct? Every section prefix must be in sections.json, every category in categories.json, every alias must point to an existing check, and a retired number may never come back. This is a check on the module itself, not on the tenant.

checks.title: CA app exclusion without an owner (full cross-check)
checks.description: Resolves every application excluded via Conditional Access to its service principal and counts the owners. Zero owners means nobody is accountable for why this app falls outside the policy. Follows on from Foundation-12, which only flags the presence of an exclusion.

checks.title: User within 'All users' scope is not MFA-capable
checks.reviewQuestion: Will this user be able to sign in once the policy enforces MFA?
checks.description: Cross-checks the users within an enabled 'All users' CA policy (minus explicit exclusions) against isMfaCapable from userRegistrationDetails. A user who is not MFA-capable gets stuck once the policy is enforced. Reporting latency in the source makes this a check to confirm, not a hard verdict.

checks.title: Service account (heuristic) within 'All users' scope
checks.reviewQuestion: Should this service account fall within the user scope?
checks.description: Cross-checks heuristically recognized service/shared accounts against the scope of an enabled 'All users' CA policy. A non-interactive account within scope can get stuck on MFA. Name heuristic, so always confirm; the same pattern recognition as Identity-02.

checks.title: Sync account excluded from CA
checks.reviewQuestion: Should the sync account be excluded from these policies?
checks.description: The account Entra Connect or Cloud Sync uses to synchronize carries the Directory Synchronization Accounts directory role. Microsoft names that account by role among the identities you exclude from blocking CA policies, and recommends selecting the role instead of the individual account. This check looks up the role holders deterministically, tests the exclusion, and removes them from the user-facing MFA-readiness checks where they would otherwise show up as false positives.

checks.title: CA requires a compliant device with no platform policy
checks.description: Cross-checks CA policies with the 'compliant device' grant control against the per-platform compliance policy coverage from 6.18. If a policy requires a compliant device for a platform with no assigned compliance policy on that platform, the control is technically unenforceable for that platform.

checks.title: Baseline MFA policy for all users
checks.description: Checks whether there is an enabled CA policy that enforces MFA (or an authentication strength) for all users. This is the most fundamental CA/Secure Score recommendation and a different question from Foundation-07: that one flags the absence of exclusions, this one flags the absence of the baseline itself.

checks.title: Microsoft-managed CA policies
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to leave this Microsoft-managed policy as is?
checks.description: Microsoft creates Conditional Access policies in the tenant itself, in report-only, and turns them on by itself no less than 30 days later unless you set them to Off. They cannot be renamed or deleted; you can only adjust the state and the exclusions. This check inventories them and tests whether the emergency accounts are excluded, so your own CA rollout doesn't get overtaken partway through by policy the customer didn't turn on themselves. Baseline security mode policies are labeled separately: those are created by the administrator and don't turn on by themselves. Note that Graph has no field that marks a managed policy; recognition relies on the name prefix Microsoft documents.

checks.title: Number of CA policies against the tenant limit
checks.reviewQuestion: Is there room for the policies you still need to create?
checks.description: A tenant can hold at most 240 Conditional Access policies. Report-only and disabled policies count toward that just as much as enabled ones, and that's the trap: a migration project stacks temporary report-only policies on top of the existing set and hits a ceiling nobody accounted for. At the limit, no more policies fit. The 80 percent warning threshold is this module's own judgment call; the limit itself is Microsoft's statement.

checks.title: PIM activation policy (MFA/justification)
checks.description: Reads the tenant-wide PIM role activation policy and checks whether MFA and justification are required when activating a privileged role. Without this requirement, a compromised account can activate a privileged role with no extra verification.

checks.title: Access reviews for privileged roles
checks.description: Checks whether periodic access review definitions are set up that assess role assignments. Without review, privileged roles accumulate unnoticed over time. Requires Entra ID Governance/P2.

checks.title: Protected actions on CA management
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to require extra verification before someone changes CA policy?
checks.description: A protected action ties an authentication context to a permission, so someone must first satisfy a Conditional Access policy before they can perform the action. Microsoft recommends this for the management of Conditional Access itself: whoever can change CA can turn off every other control, and that permission isn't tied to a role but to whoever holds it through whatever path. The check looks at whether the three management actions create, update, and delete are tied to a context.

checks.title: Guest access restriction level
checks.reviewQuestion: Should guests be able to see more than the most restricted level?
checks.description: Checks whether the guest role level is set to the most restricted level (Restricted Guest User) rather than broader access. Precheck: without guests in the tenant this does not apply, and this check shows Ready instead of a forced Review required.

checks.title: Password protection (banned password list)
checks.reviewQuestion: Is the banned password list set up the way you want?
checks.description: Checks whether banned password check is enabled and whether a custom banned password list is configured. If the tenant setting itself is missing, Microsoft default values apply; that is not a deliberate choice by the tenant, hence Review required instead of Ready.

checks.title: Smart lockout configuration
checks.reviewQuestion: Does this smart lockout setting match your risk?
checks.description: Checks whether the lockout threshold is at most 10 attempts and the lockout duration at least 60 seconds, Microsoft's own smart lockout defaults. If the tenant setting itself is missing, Microsoft default values apply (which happen to meet these thresholds); hence Review required instead of Ready.

checks.title: CA policy blocks legacy authentication
checks.description: Checks whether there is an enabled CA policy that blocks legacy authentication (exchangeActiveSync/other clientAppTypes). Condition-09 only measures observed usage; this measures whether enforcement is actually in place, regardless of current usage.

checks.title: Legacy authentication drilldown (user/app/device type)
checks.description: Only when Condition-09 actually finds legacy usage: pulls a breakdown via Log Analytics (KQL) of which users, apps, and device types use legacy authentication, so you know who needs to migrate first before you block legacy auth. Uses the exact same legacy clientApp list as Condition-09. Requires an Azure context (on by default, turn off with -SkipAzure) and a discovered Log Analytics workspace; without that context this check is skipped (no record).

checks.title: Deprecated grant control 'approved client app'
checks.reviewQuestion: Can this deprecated grant control be removed?
checks.description: Flags CA policies that use the 'approved client app' grant control. From June 30, 2026, this control and the policies containing it are read-only: they can no longer be created or changed, but can still be disabled or deleted. Existing policies keep enforcing as long as they stay enabled, so the effect is a freeze, not a silent loss of enforcement. The migration step Microsoft describes is the combination 'approved client app' OR 'app protection policy', and after that just 'app protection policy'.

checks.title: Default compliance action for unmanaged devices
checks.description: Checks whether devices with no assigned compliance policy are marked 'not compliant' by default (secureByDefault). Without this setting, such devices are silently treated as compliant, which undermines 'require compliant device' controls. Microsoft lists this among its Level 1 minimal device compliance recommendations (learn.microsoft.com/intune/fundamentals/deploy-compliance-step-3, verified 12-09-2026).

checks.title: Validity period of the compliance status
checks.reviewQuestion: Is this compliance status validity period acceptable?
checks.description: If a device doesn't report its compliance status within the configured period, Intune treats it as not compliant. The default is 30 days and it's settable from 1 to 120. A long period undermines 'require compliant device' the same way a missing secure-by-default setting does: a device that has reported nothing for months still counts as compliant and is simply let through.

checks.title: App protection policy as a CA dependency
checks.reviewQuestion: Is there app protection policy for everyone it applies to?
checks.description: The Conditional Access control 'Require app protection policy' only works together with app protection policy from Intune. If that policy doesn't exist, or is assigned to nobody, no user can satisfy the control and everyone it applies to gets blocked. In the portal, an unassigned policy looks like it's handled. The check reads the iOS and Android policies separately, since only there does it show whether a policy is actually assigned.

checks.title: App protection policy coverage across the CA target audience
checks.reviewQuestion: Do all users of this CA policy fall under an app protection policy?
checks.description: Compares per platform who falls under a CA policy that enforces app protection with who falls under an assigned app protection policy. Where Device-09 only checks whether a policy exists and whether something is assigned, this check counts whether the target audience is actually covered: a policy on all users next to a policy only assigned to a pilot group blocks everyone outside it on iOS and Android. The criterion isn't equality of groups but coverage in one direction, since broader policy than the CA scope is fine. Policies with 'one of the selected controls' don't count, except in the migration state where only approved client app remains as the alternative. Role-based targeting and nested groups cannot be expanded with certainty and therefore yield Review required instead of a hard verdict.

checks.title: BYOD enrollment restriction
checks.reviewQuestion: Should personal devices be able to enroll this way?
checks.description: Checks whether personal (BYOD) device enrollment is blocked per platform. No block means any personal device can register unless other controls catch it.

checks.title: Token Protection enforced
checks.description: Checks whether there is an enabled CA policy that enforces Token Protection (sessionControls.secureSignInSession). Microsoft's own deployment guide recommends this for Exchange Online, SharePoint Online and Teams, starting with privileged users on managed Windows devices (learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/conditional-access/deployment-guide-token-protection-windows, verified 12-09-2026); limits the impact of token theft on critical resources. The measurement prefers reading this property from the v1.0 response and only falls back to beta when v1.0 doesn't carry the field at all. If neither source carries the field, the check isn't measurable and yields Not assessed, never a Gap. A policy that carries the control but has it off doesn't count as enforced; that is named separately in the finding.

checks.title: Resilience defaults disabled
checks.description: Resilience defaults are on by default on every Conditional Access policy and keep existing sessions working during an outage of the primary authentication service. Microsoft recommends leaving them on. Turning them off on a policy targeted at a group or role reduces resilience for the whole tenant, not just that target audience, and the effect can't be tested in advance: there's no dry run via the Backup Authentication Service. That hits exactly the scenario emergency accounts exist for.

checks.title: Continuous Access Evaluation per policy
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to leave Continuous Access Evaluation as is for this policy?
checks.description: Continuous Access Evaluation revokes a session almost immediately when an account is disabled, the password changes, or risk rises; without CAE a token stays valid until it expires. It's on by default, so a policy that sets it to disabled is a deliberate weakening that deserves a reason. When a policy enables strict location enforcement, all traffic must come from known, owned egress addresses recorded as a named location; with shared or undeterminable egress you instead lock out trusted users. This setting only exists in the beta version of Graph.

checks.title: Geographic access restriction
checks.reviewQuestion: Do you want to restrict access to these countries?
checks.description: Checks whether there is a country-based named location used by a CA policy to restrict access from unexpected countries.

checks.title: Risk-based CA policy present
checks.description: Checks whether an enabled CA policy responds to sign-in risk and/or user risk. Readable independent of a P2 license (it's the CA configuration, not the risk data itself); risk detection with no policy responding to it changes nothing about the actual risk.
